scope: Educational comparisons only; diet-ranking catalogue remains unchanged.

variants.geneRole: Helps turn folate, a vitamin in foods, into a form your cells use. This supports normal cell repair and recycling of a blood chemical called homocysteine.
variants.variantMeaning: The common 677C>T protein change is written G>A on the genomic forward strand. A corresponds to 677T.
variants.evidence: Functional and biomarker evidence; nutritional outcome depends on folate status.

comparisons.GG: GG: this particular change is not present. Folate processing is usually more efficient than with AA, but this result does not prove your folate level is adequate.
comparisons.AG: AG: one copy of the change. This processing step may work less efficiently than GG, usually with a smaller effect than AA. Adequate folate intake still matters.
comparisons.AA: AA: two copies of the change. This processing step is generally less efficient. Low folate intake can make raised homocysteine more likely; you can still use food folate and folic acid.

variants.dietMeaning: Try lentils, beans, spinach or asparagus regularly. Fortified cereals or grain products can also supply folic acid; check the label.
variants.limitations: Common variation is not severe MTHFR deficiency. Food folate and folic acid can still be used; no fixed personal enzyme-activity percentage is inferred.

GG.headline: No reduced-activity copy here
GG.action: Meet normal folate needs; this result alone does not call for extra supplements.

AG.headline: Folate processing may be less efficient
AG.action: Make folate-rich foods a regular habit. Extra attention to intake is useful; a special supplement is not automatically needed.

AA.headline: Folate processing is usually less efficient
AA.action: Pay particular attention to meeting folate needs. If intake is poor or relevant blood tests are abnormal, discuss how to correct the gap.

foodSteps: Try lentils, beans, spinach or asparagus regularly.
Fortified cereals or grain products can also supply folic acid; check the label.
practicalGuidance.supplements: Folic acid still works with this variant. A methylfolate product or high dose is not automatically better. A supplement may help cover an intake gap; pregnancy guidance applies independently of this result.
practicalGuidance.followUp: If there is a clinical reason, ask about folate, B12 and homocysteine tests. Homocysteine is a blood chemical influenced by several nutrients and other health factors.

variants.geneRole: Works in the same folate-processing system as the other MTHFR marker. This is a different DNA position, so its result must be read separately.
variants.variantMeaning: A1298C changes a protein residue in the regulatory region. Forward G corresponds to gene-oriented 1298C; T corresponds to 1298A.
variants.evidence: Functional evidence; isolated biomarker effects are less consistent than for rs1801133.

comparisons.TT: TT: this particular reduced-activity change is not present. It does not tell you your result at the other MTHFR marker.
comparisons.GT: GT: one copy of the change. Some laboratory studies find an effect on the enzyme, but this result alone cannot tell us how well you use folate.
comparisons.GG: GG: two copies of the change. Lower enzyme activity has been seen in studies, but a low folate level or a need for extra supplements does not automatically follow.

variants.dietMeaning: Include beans, leafy vegetables and folate-fortified foods as part of a varied diet.
variants.limitations: The combined effect with rs1801133 requires careful interpretation; Bloom does not infer phase or a combined activity score.

TT.headline: No reduced-activity copy here
TT.action: Meet normal folate needs. No extra action is established for this result alone.

GT.headline: Practical effect is uncertain
GT.action: Keep folate intake adequate; do not assume this makes you folate deficient.

GG.headline: Lower activity is possible; diet effect is uncertain
GG.action: Keep folate intake adequate. Use actual health findings, rather than this result alone, to decide on supplements.

foodSteps: Include beans, leafy vegetables and folate-fortified foods as part of a varied diet.
practicalGuidance.supplements: No special form or dose is established for this marker. Folic acid can still be used.
practicalGuidance.followUp: Review B12, folate or homocysteine with a clinician if symptoms, diet or medical history give a reason. Bloom does not combine the two MTHFR markers into an activity score.

variants.geneRole: Helps keep a vitamin B12-dependent recycling process working. This process uses folate and helps prevent homocysteine, a normal blood chemical, from building up.
variants.variantMeaning: The common A66G variant changes Ile22 to Met. It has been studied in one-carbon metabolism.
variants.evidence: Candidate-variant/biomarker evidence; no established genotype-specific nutrient target.

comparisons.AA: AA: a common comparison result. It does not prove that your B12 or folate intake is adequate.
comparisons.AG: AG: one copy of each version. Research does not reliably show that you use B12 less efficiently or need more of it.
comparisons.GG: GG: two copies of this version. Evidence is not strong enough to call your B12 use better or worse or to set a different intake.

variants.dietMeaning: B12 options include eggs, dairy, meat or fish; plant-based options include B12-fortified foods.
variants.limitations: Enzyme-pathway involvement is different from evidence that extra B12 or methylated supplements improve outcomes for this genotype.

AA.action: Choose B12 sources that fit your diet; no additional supplement need is established from this result.

AG.headline: No proven change to B12 needs
AG.action: Choose B12 sources that fit your diet; no additional supplement need is established from this result.

GG.action: Choose B12 sources that fit your diet; no additional supplement need is established from this result.

foodSteps: B12 options include eggs, dairy, meat or fish; plant-based options include B12-fortified foods.

practicalGuidance.followUp: A clinician can assess B12 status if intake is low, symptoms occur or absorption problems are suspected.

variants.geneRole: Uses vitamin B12 and folate in a recycling step important for normal cell chemistry. This helps process a blood chemical called homocysteine.
variants.variantMeaning: A2756G changes Asp919 to Gly. The marker is studied in folate/B12-related metabolism.
variants.evidence: Candidate-variant associations; personal functional direction remains uncertain.

comparisons.AA: AA: a common comparison result. It does not prove that your B12 or folate intake is adequate.
comparisons.AG: AG: one copy of each version. Research does not reliably show that you use B12 less efficiently or need more of it.
comparisons.GG: GG: two copies of this version. Evidence is not strong enough to call your B12 use better or worse or to set a different intake.

variants.dietMeaning: B12 options include eggs, dairy, meat or fish; plant-based options include B12-fortified foods.
variants.limitations: Do not interpret a common MTR call as a diagnosis of rare methionine-synthase deficiency.

AA.action: Choose B12 sources that fit your diet; no additional supplement need is established from this result.

variants.geneRole: Helps process a blood chemical called homocysteine into other building blocks the body uses. The process uses vitamin B6.
variants.variantMeaning: C699T is a synonymous marker: it does not change the encoded amino acid. Forward A corresponds to the gene-oriented T allele.
variants.evidence: Inconsistent candidate-gene findings; insufficient evidence for a useful dietary activity ranking.

comparisons.GG: GG: this marker does not measure how fast this process runs.
comparisons.AG: AG: one A copy is not evidence of an overactive enzyme or excess sulfur or ammonia.
comparisons.AA: AA: two A copies do not show an overactive enzyme or a need to avoid sulfur-containing foods.

variants.dietMeaning: You do not need to cut out eggs, beans, broccoli or other protein/sulfur foods because of this SNP.
variants.limitations: Studies of homocysteine have not consistently supported the claimed functional effect; rare disease-causing CBS variants are a separate issue.

GG.headline: No proven reason to restrict foods
GG.action: Keep a varied diet; no low-sulfur or low-protein diet is justified by this marker.

AG.headline: No proven reason to restrict foods
AG.action: Keep a varied diet; no low-sulfur or low-protein diet is justified by this marker.

AA.headline: No proven reason to restrict foods
AA.action: Keep a varied diet; no low-sulfur or low-protein diet is justified by this marker.

foodSteps: You do not need to cut out eggs, beans, broccoli or other protein/sulfur foods because of this SNP.
practicalGuidance.supplements: No B6 or “detox” supplement is established for this result.
practicalGuidance.followUp: Investigate persistent symptoms on their own merits; this result is not an ammonia or sulfur test.

variants.geneRole: Helps put certain sugars on the gut lining. These sugars affect the environment microbes live in. This is called secretor status; it is not your blood type or a count of good bacteria.
variants.variantMeaning: The A stop allele can disable FUT2 secretor function. This marker explains a common non-secretor form in some populations.
variants.evidence: Established secretor biology; B12 associations do not directly measure usable B12.

comparisons.GG: GG: compatible with secretor status at this marker. It does not prove a healthy microbiome.
comparisons.AG: AG: one working G copy generally preserves secretor function. This is not halfway between secretor and non-secretor.
comparisons.AA: AA: compatible with non-secretor status from this common variant. This changes gut surface sugars, but is not automatically good or bad and does not prove poor B12 absorption.

variants.dietMeaning: Meet B12 needs using foods that suit you, including fortified options if you avoid animal foods.
variants.limitations: Other FUT2 variants and ancestry matter. Higher total B12 can reflect binding-protein differences rather than better cellular B12 supply.

GG.headline: Likely secretor at this marker
GG.action: Keep a varied diet; no special probiotic or B12 plan follows from this result.

AG.headline: Likely secretor at this marker
AG.action: Keep a varied diet; no special probiotic or B12 plan follows from this result.

AA.headline: Likely non-secretor at this marker
AA.action: Keep a varied diet; no special probiotic or B12 plan follows from this result.

foodSteps: Meet B12 needs using foods that suit you, including fortified options if you avoid animal foods.
practicalGuidance.supplements: Neither secretor status calls for an automatic probiotic or extra B12 supplement.
practicalGuidance.followUp: If B12 is a concern, use clinical assessment and blood results. Other variants can affect secretor status in different populations.

variants.geneRole: Helps convert shorter plant fats into longer-chain fats used by cells, including parts of the omega-3 and omega-6 pathways. Direct food sources supply some of these fats without relying on the full conversion pathway.
variants.variantMeaning: A common FADS-cluster marker associated with fatty-acid composition and inferred desaturase activity. It is distinct from rs174550.
variants.evidence: Replicated fatty-acid associations; causal variants and dietary response vary by population.

comparisons.TT: TT: associated with relatively higher activity of a fat-processing step than CC in the cited research. This is not an overall healthier-fat score.
comparisons.CT: CT: one of each version. Fatty-acid levels can differ on average, but your exact conversion efficiency cannot be read from this result.
comparisons.CC: CC: associated with lower estimated activity of this fat-processing step in some studies. This does not mean that you cannot use dietary fats.

variants.dietMeaning: Fish supplies EPA/DHA directly. If you avoid seafood, algae-derived DHA/EPA is an alternative to discuss. Walnuts, chia and flax supply ALA, a plant omega-3; they are useful foods but not equivalent to the same amount of EPA/DHA.
variants.limitations: Lipid ratios are proxies for activity. Do not extrapolate an exact ALA-to-EPA/DHA conversion percentage.

sources.title: NIH: omega-3 food and algae alternatives

TT.headline: Relatively higher estimated activity
TT.action: Include a variety of unsaturated fats; this result is not a reason to increase or avoid a whole fat group.

CT.headline: Your conversion rate is uncertain
CT.action: Include suitable omega-3 sources; a special dose is not established for this mixed result.

CC.headline: Relatively lower estimated activity
CC.action: Consider whether your diet includes direct EPA/DHA omega-3 sources, without assuming that this result proves a deficiency.

foodSteps: Fish supplies EPA/DHA directly. If you avoid seafood, algae-derived DHA/EPA is an alternative to discuss.
Walnuts, chia and flax supply ALA, a plant omega-3; they are useful foods but not equivalent to the same amount of EPA/DHA.
practicalGuidance.supplements: Algal or fish oil can be considered when appropriate for your intake and health context. The SNP does not calculate a dose or prove a supplement benefit.
practicalGuidance.followUp: A dietitian can review fat intake alongside blood lipids if needed. Marker effects vary across populations; no personal conversion percentage is calculated.

variants.geneRole: Helps convert shorter plant fats into longer-chain fats used by cells, including parts of the omega-3 and omega-6 pathways. Direct food sources supply some of these fats without relying on the full conversion pathway.
variants.variantMeaning: An intronic FADS1 marker investigated in diet trials comparing TT and CC groups.
variants.evidence: Human dietary intervention and mechanistic evidence; CT is not directly characterized by every trial.

comparisons.TT: TT: associated with higher estimated fat-processing activity than CC in the cited studies. More activity is not automatically better for every fat.
comparisons.CT: CT: research comparing only TT and CC does not establish that your response is halfway between them.
comparisons.CC: CC: associated with lower estimated fat-processing activity than TT in the cited studies. Your actual fatty-acid levels still depend on diet and other factors.

variants.dietMeaning: Fish supplies EPA/DHA directly. If you avoid seafood, algae-derived DHA/EPA is an alternative to discuss. Walnuts, chia and flax supply ALA, a plant omega-3; they are useful foods but not equivalent to the same amount of EPA/DHA.
variants.limitations: The cited trial contrasted homozygotes. No per-genotype oil dose or assured health benefit follows from those findings.

variants.geneRole: Helps turn beta-carotene, the orange pigment in carrots and similar foods, into vitamin A. Vitamin A supports vision and immune function. Vitamin A already present in foods uses a different route.
variants.variantMeaning: The R267S protein variant has been studied alongside other BCO1 variants in beta-carotene conversion.
variants.evidence: Small human functional studies; combined variants and food context matter.

comparisons.AA: AA: no T copies at this marker. This is not proof of efficient conversion because other genes and your diet also matter.
comparisons.AT: AT: one T copy. Conversion may vary, but studies do not establish an exact reduction from this marker alone.
comparisons.TT: TT: two T copies. Research suggests conversion can be less efficient in some genetic combinations; this single result cannot quantify the effect.

variants.dietMeaning: Carrots, sweet potatoes and leafy greens provide vitamin A precursors. Eggs, dairy and foods fortified with preformed vitamin A supply a form that does not require beta-carotene conversion; check labels.
variants.limitations: Large conversion percentages reported for combined variants must not be assigned to rs12934922 alone; this call does not diagnose vitamin A deficiency.

variants.topic: Turning plant colour into vitamin A

AA.headline: No reduced-conversion copy here
AA.action: Meet normal vitamin A needs from a varied diet; extra retinol is not indicated by this result.

AT.headline: Conversion effect is uncertain
AT.action: Review vitamin A sources if your diet is very restricted; this result alone does not establish a supplement need.

TT.headline: Possibly less efficient plant conversion
TT.action: If nearly all your vitamin A comes from plant pigments, review intake rather than assuming carrots alone cover your needs.

foodSteps: Carrots, sweet potatoes and leafy greens provide vitamin A precursors.
Eggs, dairy and foods fortified with preformed vitamin A supply a form that does not require beta-carotene conversion; check labels.
practicalGuidance.supplements: Do not start high-dose retinol from this SNP. Too much preformed vitamin A can be harmful, especially during pregnancy; a restricted vegan diet may warrant dietitian advice.
practicalGuidance.followUp: Review intake and symptoms with a clinician or dietitian if deficiency is a concern. No fixed conversion loss is assigned.

variants.geneRole: Helps the liver turn vitamin D from food, supplements and sunlight into the main form measured in blood. Vitamin D helps the body use calcium for bones and muscles.
variants.variantMeaning: A common regulatory-region marker associated with the blood vitamin D biomarker.
variants.evidence: Large human GWAS; individual supplement response is not determined by the marker.

comparisons.AA: AA: associated with higher average blood vitamin D than G-carrying groups. This is relatively favourable for that blood marker, but does not guarantee enough vitamin D.
comparisons.AG: AG: associated with a modest tendency toward lower blood vitamin D than AA. This does not prove poor absorption or a vitamin D deficiency.
comparisons.GG: GG: associated with lower average blood vitamin D than AA. It is a reason to pay attention to intake and context, not proof that dietary vitamin D cannot be used.

variants.dietMeaning: Use vitamin D-fortified milk or plant drinks, eggs or fatty fish as suitable for your diet.
variants.limitations: Season, sun exposure, body composition and other genes can outweigh the contribution of this marker.

sources.title: NIH: vitamin D, food, supplements and sunlight

AA.headline: Relatively higher vitamin D levels on average
AA.action: Meet normal vitamin D needs; do not skip vitamin D sources just because this result is favourable.

AG.headline: Slight tendency toward lower vitamin D levels
AG.action: Check whether your usual diet supplies vitamin D. Consider supplement needs based on intake and clinical context.

GG.headline: Tendency toward lower vitamin D levels
GG.action: Pay attention to vitamin D intake, especially if you have other reasons for low levels. Discuss testing when clinically appropriate; no higher dose follows automatically.

foodSteps: Use vitamin D-fortified milk or plant drinks, eggs or fatty fish as suitable for your diet.
practicalGuidance.supplements: A vitamin D supplement can cover an intake gap or treat a confirmed low level with appropriate advice. This marker does not choose a dose. More unprotected sun is not a recommended fix; sunlight-derived vitamin D also needs processing.
practicalGuidance.followUp: If testing is appropriate, the usual status test is 25-hydroxyvitamin D. Routine testing is not needed for every healthy person; intake, bone health and medical history matter.

variants.geneRole: Helps turn stored/circulating vitamin D into an active hormone, mainly in the kidneys. This is a different step from absorbing vitamin D from food.
variants.variantMeaning: A promoter-region marker, often written -1260C>A in gene-oriented notation; forward alleles are G/T.
variants.evidence: Candidate-variant and functional-context evidence; dietary actionability is limited.

comparisons.GG: GG: this result does not tell us whether you activate vitamin D more or less efficiently.
comparisons.GT: GT: no reliable halfway activation rate has been established for this result.
comparisons.TT: TT: this result does not reliably predict active vitamin D levels or a different supplement need.

variants.dietMeaning: Vitamin D-fortified foods can help cover intake; this result does not make them unusable.
variants.limitations: Candidate studies do not establish a general-population genotype-specific dose or a simple universal best genotype.

GG.action: Meet normal vitamin D needs. Do not treat this as a blocked activation pathway.

GT.headline: Activation efficiency is not known from this SNP
GT.action: Meet normal vitamin D needs. Do not treat this as a blocked activation pathway.

TT.headline: Activation efficiency is not known from this SNP
TT.action: Meet normal vitamin D needs. Do not treat this as a blocked activation pathway.

foodSteps: Vitamin D-fortified foods can help cover intake; this result does not make them unusable.
practicalGuidance.supplements: Do not start prescription active vitamin D (calcitriol) or high doses from this SNP.
practicalGuidance.followUp: Kidney problems or abnormal calcium/vitamin D results need clinical interpretation. This SNP alone is not a reason for routine extra tests.

variants.geneRole: Helps the body control how much iron enters from food. Iron is essential, but excessive buildup can damage organs.
variants.variantMeaning: The A allele encodes C282Y, an important hereditary-haemochromatosis variant.
variants.evidence: Established clinical relevance; penetrance is incomplete and context dependent.

comparisons.GG: GG: no C282Y change at this marker. It does not rule out iron overload or iron deficiency.
comparisons.AG: AG: one C282Y copy. Most people with just one copy do not develop iron overload from this alone. Other variants and blood tests matter.
comparisons.AA: AA: two C282Y copies can weaken the brake on iron absorption. This needs clinical confirmation and assessment, but not everyone develops iron-overload disease.

variants.dietMeaning: Do not automatically eliminate meat, beans or leafy greens. Confirmed iron overload calls for an individual plan.
variants.limitations: Sex, age, ancestry, other variants and environmental factors affect expression. No diagnosis or penetrance percentage is assigned to the individual.

sources.title: NIDDK: diet when iron overload is diagnosed

GG.headline: No C282Y copy here
GG.action: Eat normally and base iron treatment on measured need.

AG.headline: One C282Y copy; overload is not established
AG.action: A restrictive low-iron diet is not automatically needed. Ask about iron testing if family history or other findings raise concern.

AA.headline: Higher iron-overload susceptibility
AA.action: Discuss this with a clinician for clinical confirmation and blood iron assessment before changing diet or supplements.

foodSteps: Do not automatically eliminate meat, beans or leafy greens. Confirmed iron overload calls for an individual plan.
practicalGuidance.supplements: Do not start iron just because you feel tired. If iron overload is confirmed, avoid non-prescribed iron and vitamin C supplements; discuss existing prescriptions before changing them.
practicalGuidance.followUp: Ferritin checks stored iron; transferrin saturation helps show how much circulating iron is carried. A clinician interprets them together, because ferritin can rise for other reasons.

variants.geneRole: Helps the body control how much iron enters from food. Iron is essential, but excessive buildup can damage organs.
variants.variantMeaning: The G allele encodes H63D. Its clinical significance differs from the separate C282Y variant.
variants.evidence: Established variant identity; standalone clinical effects are smaller and context dependent.

comparisons.CC: CC: no H63D change at this marker. It does not prove your iron level is normal.
comparisons.CG: CG: one H63D copy usually does not cause iron overload on its own.
comparisons.GG: GG: two H63D copies may influence iron measures, but usually have a much smaller clinical effect than two C282Y copies. Do not assume you have excess iron.

variants.dietMeaning: Do not automatically eliminate meat, beans or leafy greens. Confirmed iron overload calls for an individual plan.
variants.limitations: One H63D and one C282Y result does not establish which chromosome each is on. No compound-haplotype diagnosis is inferred.

sources.title: NIDDK: diet when iron overload is diagnosed

CC.headline: No H63D copy here
CC.action: No special iron restriction follows from this marker.

CG.headline: Usually little effect on its own
CG.action: Do not cut out iron-rich foods from this result alone.

GG.headline: Iron status matters more than this call
GG.action: Review any other HFE results and measured iron status before changing intake.

foodSteps: Do not automatically eliminate meat, beans or leafy greens. Confirmed iron overload calls for an individual plan.
practicalGuidance.supplements: Do not start iron just because you feel tired. If iron overload is confirmed, avoid non-prescribed iron and vitamin C supplements; discuss existing prescriptions before changing them.
practicalGuidance.followUp: Ferritin checks stored iron; transferrin saturation helps show how much circulating iron is carried. A clinician interprets them together, because ferritin can rise for other reasons.

variants.geneRole: Helps control hepcidin, a hormone that acts as a brake on iron absorption and release. This affects iron available for red blood cells.
variants.variantMeaning: A common protein-changing marker associated with iron and haemoglobin traits.
variants.evidence: Replicated biomarker associations and a human iron-absorption study.

comparisons.GG: GG: relatively higher average iron measures than A-carrying groups. This does not guarantee normal iron status.
comparisons.AG: AG: a modest tendency toward lower iron-related blood measures than GG. This is not an iron-deficiency diagnosis.
comparisons.AA: AA: a stronger tendency toward lower iron-related measures in some studies. Actual need for treatment depends on blood tests.

variants.dietMeaning: Iron sources include beans, lentils, fortified cereals and meat if eaten. Combine plant iron with vitamin C foods, such as peppers or citrus, to help absorption.
variants.limitations: Effects vary by ancestry and physiological context. This common variant is different from rare causes of iron-refractory anaemia.

GG.headline: No lower-iron A copy here
GG.action: Meet normal iron needs; no extra supplement is indicated by the genotype.

AG.headline: Slight tendency toward lower iron measures
AG.action: Include regular iron sources and investigate low iron if there are symptoms or other reasons for concern.

AA.headline: Tendency toward lower iron measures
AA.action: Review iron intake and possible blood testing if you have fatigue, heavy bleeding or another deficiency risk.

foodSteps: Iron sources include beans, lentils, fortified cereals and meat if eaten.
Combine plant iron with vitamin C foods, such as peppers or citrus, to help absorption.
practicalGuidance.supplements: Use iron supplements for measured or clinician-assessed need, not this SNP alone. Excess iron can be harmful.
practicalGuidance.followUp: Haemoglobin measures oxygen-carrying blood cells; ferritin helps assess iron stores. Other results may be needed to explain an abnormal value.

variants.geneRole: Helps control how the pancreas releases insulin, the hormone that moves sugar from the blood into cells.
variants.variantMeaning: A common regulatory marker associated with type 2 diabetes susceptibility.
variants.evidence: Strong human genetic association; genotype-specific food prescriptions are unproven.

comparisons.CC: CC: lower average diabetes susceptibility than T-carrying groups at this marker. Healthy habits and blood sugar checks still matter.
comparisons.CT: CT: one T copy is associated with greater type 2 diabetes susceptibility than CC. It does not mean you have diabetes or cannot eat carbohydrates.
comparisons.TT: TT: two T copies generally have a stronger association with type 2 diabetes susceptibility. Your actual blood sugar cannot be predicted from this alone.

variants.dietMeaning: Choose high-fibre carbohydrate foods; replace sugary drinks with unsweetened options.
variants.limitations: The table covers the studied C/T pair. Other reported alleles are held for review rather than silently translated.

sources.title: NIDDK: eating and activity for blood sugar

CC.headline: Lower susceptibility at this marker
CC.action: Use normal blood-sugar-friendly habits; no special carbohydrate restriction is established for this call.

CT.headline: Higher blood-sugar susceptibility
CT.action: Give blood-sugar-friendly habits attention and use actual measurements to decide whether anything more is needed.

TT.headline: Higher blood-sugar susceptibility
TT.action: Give blood-sugar-friendly habits attention and discuss screening based on your overall risk, not a genetic calorie or carbohydrate formula.

foodSteps: Choose high-fibre carbohydrate foods; replace sugary drinks with unsweetened options.
practicalGuidance.supplements: No supplement is proven necessary from this marker.
practicalGuidance.followUp: HbA1c reflects average blood sugar over roughly three months. A clinician can decide whether HbA1c or fasting glucose testing is appropriate.

variants.geneRole: Helps cells respond to melatonin, the hormone that signals night-time. It also affects insulin release, linking the body clock with blood sugar.
variants.variantMeaning: The G allele at this intronic marker is associated with higher fasting glucose and a weaker early insulin response.
variants.evidence: Replicated human GWAS and insulin-secretion studies.

comparisons.CC: CC: lower average fasting blood sugar than G-carrying groups in the cited research. This is not protection against diabetes.
comparisons.CG: CG: one G copy is linked to slightly higher fasting blood sugar and a weaker early insulin response on average.
comparisons.GG: GG: two G copies are linked to a larger average shift in these blood sugar measures. The result does not predict your reaction to an individual meal.

variants.dietMeaning: Use balanced meals with fibre-rich foods and limit sugary drinks as generally appropriate.
variants.limitations: A population-average association does not determine an individual response to a particular meal or melatonin dose.

sources.title: NIDDK: eating and activity for blood sugar

CC.headline: No glucose-raising G copy here
CC.action: Keep consistent sleep and eating habits; no genotype-specific eating cutoff is established.

CG.headline: Slight tendency toward higher fasting glucose
CG.action: Keep consistent sleep and eating habits; no genotype-specific eating cutoff is established.

GG.headline: Tendency toward higher fasting glucose
GG.action: Keep consistent sleep and eating habits; no genotype-specific eating cutoff is established.

foodSteps: Use balanced meals with fibre-rich foods and limit sugary drinks as generally appropriate.
practicalGuidance.supplements: Do not start or stop melatonin from this SNP alone. Discuss sleep supplements if blood sugar or medication use is a concern.
practicalGuidance.followUp: Use actual fasting glucose or HbA1c (a measure of average blood sugar over roughly three months) when testing is indicated. A rigid rule such as “never eat after 6 pm” cannot be calculated from this result.

variants.geneRole: Helps absorb vitamin C in the gut and keep it from being lost through the kidneys. Vitamin C supports normal tissues and helps absorb plant iron.
variants.variantMeaning: A protein-changing marker associated with circulating vitamin C; the studied forward T allele is the vitamin-C-lowering allele.
variants.evidence: Replicated human biomarker association; clinical supplement benefit is not established.

comparisons.CC: CC: no vitamin-C-lowering T copy here. A low-fruit-and-vegetable diet can still leave intake too low.
comparisons.CT: CT: linked to lower average blood vitamin C than CC. It does not show how much you personally absorb or prove a deficiency.
comparisons.TT: TT: an uncommon result with limited precision in studies. It may affect vitamin C levels, but a personal supplement requirement is not established.

variants.dietMeaning: Try peppers, citrus, kiwifruit, berries or broccoli across your meals.
variants.limitations: A biomarker association does not establish that increasing a supplement dose improves health outcomes.

variants.geneRole: Marks a DNA region involved in appetite and weight regulation. It does not measure how many calories you burn.
variants.variantMeaning: An intronic association marker. It tags a larger regulatory region rather than providing a direct calorie-burn measurement.
variants.evidence: Replicated obesity association; appetite findings and effect size depend on context.

comparisons.TT: TT: lower average weight-gain susceptibility than A-carrying groups at this marker. It does not protect against weight gain.
comparisons.AT: AT: linked to a modest average tendency toward higher body weight. It does not prove a slow metabolism or that you cannot lose weight.
comparisons.AA: AA: usually a stronger average weight association than one A copy. Your hunger, habits and weight trajectory matter much more for practical planning.

variants.dietMeaning: Build meals around a protein source and fibre-rich foods; plan portions that fit your observed hunger.
variants.limitations: The marker does not explain all appetite differences and is not a test of willpower. Associations are not destiny.

variants.geneRole: Is involved in a liver hormone that helps signal nutrient needs and food preferences. This marker has been linked to differences in sweet-food intake.
variants.variantMeaning: A common synonymous marker associated with the proportion of carbohydrate/sweet foods consumed in human studies.
variants.evidence: Human dietary-preference associations; causal mechanism and intervention utility remain uncertain.

comparisons.GG: GG: the comparison group in the cited food-intake research. It does not mean you have no sweet preferences.
comparisons.AG: AG: linked to higher reported sugar or carbohydrate intake in some studies. This is a tendency, not proof of cravings or a need for sugar.
comparisons.AA: AA: does not establish stronger cravings than AG or show that extra sugar is needed. The evidence cannot set a personal sugar limit.

variants.dietMeaning: If sweet drinks or snacks dominate your diet, try unsweetened drinks and planned alternatives such as whole fruit.
variants.limitations: A synonymous marker can tag a regulatory effect elsewhere. It is not a direct hormone-level test.

variants.geneRole: Makes part of a cell-protection system that handles reactive oxygen chemicals inside cells. Its first step produces another chemical that other enzymes must then clear.
variants.variantMeaning: A protein change in the mitochondrial targeting sequence; forward A corresponds to Val and G to Ala at the commonly described position 16.
variants.evidence: Functional cell/protein evidence; clinical diet translation is uncertain.

comparisons.AA: AA: one laboratory-studied version of the protein. This is not a direct measure of oxidative stress or overall antioxidant protection.
comparisons.AG: AG: a mix of the two protein versions. A halfway antioxidant requirement has not been established.
comparisons.GG: GG: this version can behave differently in laboratory studies, but that does not make it universally better or prove that you need more antioxidants.

variants.dietMeaning: Eat a variety of vegetables and fruit rather than trying to match an antioxidant product to this SNP.
variants.limitations: Both reactive-oxygen production and clearance are complex; no personal oxidative-stress score or longevity estimate is inferred.

variants.geneRole: Helps make a protein that travels with blood fats. A common change near this gene has been studied for its relationship with saturated-fat intake and body weight.
variants.variantMeaning: A promoter variant studied for interactions with saturated fat. Forward G corresponds to the gene-oriented -265C allele; forward A corresponds to -265T.
variants.evidence: Replicated observational gene–diet interaction; no individually validated threshold.

comparisons.AA: AA: grouped in the lower-susceptibility comparison group in the cited diet studies. A high-saturated-fat diet can still be unhealthy.
comparisons.AG: AG: grouped with AA in the key study comparison, not assumed halfway to GG. No extra sensitivity to saturated fat is established from this result.
comparisons.GG: GG: associated with higher body weight particularly when saturated-fat intake was high in several studies. This is a possible susceptibility, not proof of a personal response.

variants.dietMeaning: Use olive or canola oil instead of butter; consider leaner proteins or beans instead of fatty meats.
variants.limitations: The comparison is conditional on diet and study design, not a universal ranking of good and bad genotypes.

AA.action: Follow general heart-healthy fat guidance; this result does not make high saturated-fat intake harmless.

AG.action: Follow general heart-healthy fat guidance; no stricter genotype-specific target is established.

GG.action: Give saturated-fat sources attention, while recognising that a special personal cutoff is not validated.

practicalGuidance.supplements: No supplement is established to offset this result.
practicalGuidance.followUp: Use blood lipids, actual food intake and weight trends to assess whether changes are helping.

variants.geneRole: Helps handle fats inside liver cells. The studied change can make fat more likely to build up in the liver.
variants.variantMeaning: The G allele encodes the I148M change associated with increased liver-fat susceptibility.
variants.evidence: Strong human association and functional evidence; expression depends on other factors.

comparisons.CC: CC: lower average liver-fat susceptibility than G-carrying groups at this marker. Fatty liver can still occur.
comparisons.CG: CG: one G copy is associated with increased liver-fat susceptibility. It does not diagnose fatty liver or predict its severity.
comparisons.GG: GG: two G copies generally show a stronger liver-fat association. This deserves attention to liver health, but is not a diagnosis or a measure of liver scarring.

variants.dietMeaning: Limit sugary drinks. If fatty liver is present, discuss alcohol use and sustainable weight management when appropriate.
variants.limitations: Actual liver fat, inflammation and fibrosis cannot be determined from the genotype.

CC.action: Use general liver-healthy habits; test or treat based on overall health findings.

CG.action: Pay attention to liver health, particularly if other metabolic or liver findings are present.

GG.action: Discuss liver assessment when appropriate to your medical context. No supplement can be chosen from this result alone.

foodSteps: Limit sugary drinks. If fatty liver is present, discuss alcohol use and sustainable weight management when appropriate.
practicalGuidance.supplements: No “liver detox” supplement is established for this SNP.
practicalGuidance.followUp: Liver blood tests and, when indicated, imaging assess actual liver health. Normal enzymes alone do not exclude liver fat.

variants.geneRole: Helps liver cells package and send fat into the blood. Less efficient export can leave more fat in the liver even when blood cholesterol is lower.
variants.variantMeaning: The T allele encodes E167K and is associated with liver-fat and circulating-lipid differences.
variants.evidence: Replicated human association with functional support.

comparisons.CC: CC: the comparison result at this marker. It does not rule out fatty liver or high cholesterol.
comparisons.CT: CT: one T copy is linked to less efficient fat export, more liver fat and often lower blood lipids on average. The trade-off is not simply good or bad.
comparisons.TT: TT: two T copies are uncommon. Liver-fat susceptibility can be increased, but the exact personal effect cannot be calculated from this result.

variants.dietMeaning: Use general liver-healthy food habits, including fewer sugary drinks. Avoid trying to “flush out” liver fat with supplements.
variants.limitations: No individual dietary response or diagnosis follows from this marker alone.

variants.geneRole: Helps control how the liver handles glucose, a form of sugar. A change in this control system can push blood sugar and triglycerides in different directions.
variants.variantMeaning: The T allele encodes P446L and is associated with higher triglycerides but lower fasting glucose on average.
variants.evidence: Replicated human metabolic-trait association.

comparisons.CC: CC: the comparison group at this marker. It does not prove healthy glucose or triglyceride levels.
comparisons.CT: CT: linked to slightly lower fasting glucose but higher triglycerides on average. A lower sugar reading does not necessarily mean the whole metabolic picture is better.
comparisons.TT: TT: generally a larger average shift toward lower fasting glucose and higher triglycerides. Your actual levels still require measurement.

variants.dietMeaning: Reduce sugary drinks and excess added sugar if these are common in your diet.
variants.limitations: This is not a genetic carbohydrate limit, insulin-resistance diagnosis or reason for a particular supplement.

variants.geneRole: Helps control whether the gut keeps making lactase in adulthood. Lactase is the enzyme that breaks down lactose, the sugar in milk.
variants.variantMeaning: A marker in an MCM6 regulatory region influences the neighbouring LCT gene. Forward A corresponds to the commonly described persistence-associated -13910T allele.
variants.evidence: Established functional association in relevant ancestry groups; symptoms depend on more than this SNP.

comparisons.GG: GG: compatible with making less lactase as an adult. Milk sugar may be harder to digest, but symptoms depend on the amount eaten and other factors.
comparisons.AG: AG: one persistence-associated A copy is generally sufficient to keep making lactase in adulthood. It is not necessarily a halfway ability to digest milk.
comparisons.AA: AA: compatible with continuing lactase production in adulthood. Milk sugar is usually easier to digest, but this does not rule out other reasons for dairy symptoms.

variants.dietMeaning: If needed, try lactose-free milk, yogurt or hard cheese in amounts you tolerate. If avoiding dairy, choose alternatives that supply calcium and vitamin D, such as suitably fortified plant drinks.
variants.limitations: Other lactase-persistence variants occur in different populations. Milk allergy, lactose intolerance and other digestive problems are different conditions.

GG.headline: Milk sugar may be harder to digest
GG.action: If dairy causes symptoms, try a smaller portion or lower-lactose options; there is no need to ban all dairy automatically.

AG.headline: Usually keeps lactase in adulthood
AG.action: No lactose restriction is needed from the genotype alone. Use your actual tolerance.

AA.headline: Usually keeps lactase in adulthood
AA.action: No lactose restriction is needed from the genotype alone. Investigate persistent symptoms rather than assuming the DNA rules them out.

foodSteps: If needed, try lactose-free milk, yogurt or hard cheese in amounts you tolerate.
If avoiding dairy, choose alternatives that supply calcium and vitamin D, such as suitably fortified plant drinks.
practicalGuidance.supplements: Lactase enzyme products can help some people with lactose-related symptoms; they are different from vitamin supplements. This is not treatment for a milk allergy.
practicalGuidance.followUp: Persistent symptoms deserve assessment. Other lactase-persistence variants occur in different populations, so this marker is not universal.
